claims.text: TaVCrW is a refractory high-entropy alloy.
The solid TaVCrW alloy is a disordered BCC solid solution.
The TaVCrW solid phase can develop short-range order.
An MTP trained on TaVCrW DFT data over 2000-2400 K can accurately represent both solid and liquid configurations.
Replacing EAM with an MTP and TI with FEP will reduce computational cost by more than 80% relative to TOR-TILD.
The MTP+FEP method will maintain sub-meV free-energy accuracy.
Accurate reproduction of the ab initio phase-space distributions of the solid and complex liquid enables rapid FEP convergence without a thermodynamic-integration path.
The relevant phase-space representation includes local atomic environments, solid-state SRO, and the disordered liquid structure.
The MTP supplies a computationally inexpensive surrogate for the DFT energy landscape.
FEP can calculate the solid-liquid free-energy difference by sampling configurations from the MTP reference state.
SRO stabilizes the TaVCrW solid by approximately 2-3 meV/atom.
Training the MTP on DFT data captures electronic-excitation or density-of-states-gap effects relevant to melting.
The TaVCrW melting point will lie between 2300 and 2450 K after accounting for SRO stabilization.
The calculated TaVCrW melting temperature will have uncertainty below 5 K.
A supercell larger than 128 atoms is required to converge the SRO contribution and finite-size effects.
Validation over 2000-2400 K is sufficient to cover the expected melting regime.
Magnetic fluctuations are negligible for TaVCrW under the proposed conditions.
Insufficient liquid-phase training data may cause MTP extrapolation errors, and neglected Cr magnetic fluctuations may contribute additional error.
NbMoTaW is a suitable simpler refractory-alloy benchmark for comparison of MTP+FEP with TOR-TILD.
The hypothesis is falsified if the MTP+FEP free-energy result differs from TOR-TILD by more than 0.5 meV/atom at melting or if cost reduction is below 80%.

contradictions.description: The conditions specify a minimum supercell of 128 atoms or larger, whereas the boundary states that validity requires more than 128 atoms; exactly 128 atoms is therefore both allowed and excluded.
The 2000-2400 K range is said to cover the expected melting point, but the predicted melting interval extends to 2450 K.

The predicted outcome states uncertainty below 5 K, while the uncertainty field permits a deviation of ±10 K if the liquid structure is not captured; the unconditional headline uncertainty is not reconciled with this larger conditional error.
